title: Dual-Mode Execution and Privilege Rings
summary: The hardware distinguishes exactly two execution modes — kernel and user — and enforces which instructions and memory each one can touch, the single mechanism every other OS-level protection guarantee in this discipline is ultimately built from.

references.label: MIT 6.S081 — OS Organization and System Calls

title: Traps, Interrupts, and Exceptions
summary: A system call, a hardware interrupt, and a page fault look completely different to the programmer, but the CPU handles all three with the exact same trap mechanism — save the current state, jump to a fixed kernel entry point, and let the kernel sort out why it was called.

references.label: MIT 6.S081 xv6 book — Traps, Interrupts, and Drivers

title: Anatomy of a System Call

related.label: The Process API: fork() and exec()

summary: Tracing a single call like write() from a user-space library wrapper through the trap instruction, into the kernel's system-call table, through the actual kernel routine, and back — the concrete machinery behind every OS service a program ever asks for.

references.label: MIT 6.S081 xv6 book — Traps, Interrupts, and Drivers

title: Validating User Input at the Kernel Boundary
summary: Every pointer and length a user program hands to a system call is a claim the kernel cannot trust — the same memory-safety failure mode already seen at the application level becomes catastrophic here, because the code trusting bad input is running with full privilege.

references.label: MIT 6.S081 xv6 book — Traps, Interrupts, and Drivers

title: Pipes and Anonymous Communication
summary: The shell's | operator connects one process's standard output directly to another's standard input through a kernel-managed byte buffer — the simplest, oldest, and still most common form of IPC on any Unix-like system.

title: Shared Memory IPC
summary: The kernel maps the exact same physical page into two otherwise-isolated address spaces, giving both processes direct, zero-copy access to the same bytes — the fastest IPC mechanism there is, and the one that hands all synchronization responsibility straight back to the already-covered lock and semaphore mechanics.

title: Message Queues and Structured IPC
summary: Instead of a raw shared buffer or an undifferentiated byte stream, the kernel manages discrete, typed messages with their own delivery and ordering guarantees — trading shared memory's raw speed for safety, since the kernel mediates every access instead of trusting processes to coordinate correctly on their own.

title: Sockets as a Uniform IPC Abstraction
summary: The Berkeley sockets API presents communication with a process on the same machine and a process on the other side of the planet through the exact same read/write interface — the abstraction this discipline's IPC mechanisms converge on, and the one a future networking discipline builds directly on top of.

references.label: MIT 6.S081 — OS Organization and System Calls

title: Full-System Virtualization and Hypervisors
summary: A hypervisor runs an entire guest operating system — kernel, drivers, and all — as if it had a whole machine to itself, by intercepting every privileged instruction the guest tries to execute and emulating its effect instead of letting it touch the real hardware.

references.label: Popek & Goldberg — Formal Requirements for Virtualizable Third Generation Architectures

title: Hardware-Assisted Virtualization
summary: Trap-and-emulate alone could not virtualize the real x86 instruction set, because a handful of privileged instructions failed to trap at all when run in user mode — the real reason Intel VT-x and AMD-V added a second privilege dimension purpose-built for hypervisors.

references.label: Popek & Goldberg — Formal Requirements for Virtualizable Third Generation Architectures

title: Containers and OS-Level Virtualization
summary: A container shares the host's single kernel and gets its isolated view of processes, network interfaces, and mounts entirely from namespaces, with cgroups capping the resources it can consume — no guest kernel to boot, which is exactly why containers start in milliseconds where a virtual machine takes seconds.

title: Access Control Lists and Unix Permissions
summary: An access control list attaches to each object the exact list of subjects allowed to touch it and how — Unix's read/write/execute permission bits are a deliberately simplified, three-bucket version of this idea, and the concrete mechanism the OS uses to enforce the authorization policies already discussed abstractly elsewhere.

references.label: ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Operating Systems Knowledge Area

title: Capability-Based Security
summary: Instead of asking an object's ACL whether a subject may act on it, a capability is an unforgeable ticket a process already holds that proves it may — a genuinely different model, real in systems like seL4, that sidesteps the classic confused-deputy problem an ACL-based design is prone to.

references.label: ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Operating Systems Knowledge Area

title: Sandboxing and the Principle of Least Privilege
summary: chroot, seccomp, and dropping setuid privileges are all the same real idea applied at different granularities — give a running process the absolute minimum access it needs to do its job, so that if it is ever compromised, the blast radius is small on purpose, not by luck.

title: Capstone: Tracing a Container Launch and Comparing Isolation Boundaries
summary: Following a single `docker run` from the shell's fork/exec through namespace and cgroup setup to the sandboxed process's first system call ties together every cluster in this discipline — and closes with an honest, numeric comparison of how much isolation a container, a VM, and a bare process each actually buy, and at what cost.

references.label: MIT 6.S081 xv6 book — Traps, Interrupts, and Drivers
